Decoding Linguistic Evolution

Causal AI for the Diachronic Dating of Ancient Akkadian
M.Sc. Thesis · Yarin Beer · HUJI Computer Science
Advisors: Prof. Nathan Wasserman · Dr. Barak Sober · Prof. Gabriel Stanovsky
What follows is the evaluation method we built and what it revealed — not a list of next steps.
The question

Can a language model actually date Akkadian — or only pretend to?

The goal
3,000 years of Akkadian literature is largely undated. Dating is, in part, a distributional problem — features that change in frequency over time — so language models should be able to help.
The catch
A model can score well by exploiting corpus artifacts — royal names, formulaic openings, archive provenance — without representing linguistic change at all.
Our real question
Do the model's representations carry a causally grounded diachronic signal, or only an apparent one? Telling these two apart is the whole methodological problem — and the reason we built the protocol in this talk.
How we got here · 1

Period classification looks solved

Take awayA simple linear probe on Qwen separates Old Babylonian / Neo-Assyrian / Late Babylonian letters at ~98% accuracy — but “looking solved” is exactly the trap, because this signal could be royal names and formulae, not language.
Letters corpus, 4,957 texts, 3 periods. tier0 ≈ 98%, maximal cleaning ≈ 87–93%, still above the n-gram baselines — so something real is there, but what?
How we got here · 2

Strip the artifacts and the easy clusters blur

Take awayWhen we aggressively clean the text (maximal: remove names, logograms, determinatives, formulae), the crisp left-panel period clusters dissolve on the right — evidence that much of the easy “dating” was riding on surface cues.
t-SNE of the same Qwen layer. Left = tier0 (clean OB/NA/LB blobs). Right = maximal cleaning (periods overlap). This is why we needed a harder, artifact-controlled protocol.
The method we developed

The maximal-balanced PLS protocol

Our evaluation is five deliberate choices. Each one closes a specific door a model could use to fake a date — this is the core methodological contribution.
PLS
Partial Least-Squares
Collapses each model's 4,096-dim activations onto the few latent directions aligned with the date axis. Solves: high dimensionality — finds the diachronic direction instead of overfitting noise.
ρ
Spearman correlation
Scores the ordering of predicted vs. true dates, not the exact year. Solves: dating is ordinal, and one scale-free number lets us compare a 400M encoder against a 120B decoder fairly.
μ
Mean pooling
Averages over all tokens rather than reading the last one. Solves: Akkadian is many short syllabic tokens — the document-level signal lives in the average.
✂
Maximal cleaning
Removes royal names, logograms, determinatives and formulae. Solves: separates apparent dating ability from causal linguistic signal.
⚖
Balanced (200 MC draws)
Monte-Carlo resampling + GroupKFold by ruler. Solves: 76% of fragments are three Sargonid kings — stops a model from scoring high by just guessing the majority, and blocks ruler leakage across folds.
Why balanced · 1

The imbalance trap

Take awayBecause three Sargonid kings make up 76% of the dated corpus, a dummy that just guesses the median date already looks accurate — so raw accuracy is meaningless and we had to score differently.
Accuracy@±N years vs. a predict-the-mean dummy (grey). Real models barely clear the dummy at most tolerances — the metric, not the model, is the problem.
Why balanced · 2

Where a real model actually earns its keep

Take awayBalanced scoring exposes the truth: the dummy owns the crowded centre of the timeline, and a genuine model only pulls ahead at the chronological extremes — which is exactly where dating is hard and valuable.
Right panel: median error by true date. Thalesian wins the early/late extremes; TF-IDF only beats the dummy in the dense Sargonid centre.
The headline result

A 400M model beats every giant

Take awayUnder our honest protocol, a 400M translation-finetuned model (Thalesian) tops every LLM up to 120B — and a Qwen with fully random weights ties the trained giants, so scale and pretraining are not what's doing the dating.
Balanced, maximal, best-layer year-PLS Spearman. Thalesian 0.411 > Qwen3-8B 0.363 > 32B 0.340 > gpt-oss-120B 0.333; random floor 0.301; vanilla uMT5 (no finetune) 0.297.
The finetune analysis · 1

Scale and next-token finetuning add nothing

Take awayGrowing the model to 120B, or finetuning it on Akkadian with next-token prediction, lands every arm right on top of its untouched base — more parameters and more exposure buy no dating signal.
Each “+NTP (ft)” bar sits within noise of its base bar. The lever is clearly not size and not raw next-token exposure.
The finetune analysis · 2

Next-token finetuning is a no-op, layer by layer

Take awayAcross every layer, the next-token-finetuned Qwen curves sit exactly on the base curve — confirming it's the training objective, not the amount of Akkadian seen, that's missing.
Qwen3-8B, all NTP checkpoints (ft00–ft32) overlay the base. This is what sends us toward a translation/seq2seq objective instead.
The tokenizer analysis

It is not the tokenizer either

Take awayThalesian wins despite having the least efficient Akkadian tokenizer of the whole group — it spends the most tokens per word — so cheaper or smarter tokenization is not the explanation.
Fertility = tokens per Akkadian word (lower = better). Thalesian is highest on every corpus; the win survives a worse tokenizer.
What carries the win

The translation finetune builds the signal

Take awayThe un-finetuned uMT5 base sits at the random floor and decays with depth; only the cuneiform translation finetune grows a dating representation that deepens through the network — the objective that aligns surface text with meaning is what matters.
Depth profile. uMT5 base (red) peaks at the embedding layer then falls below floor; Thalesian (green) rises to 0.41 at layer 10. Δ finetune = +0.114.
What we learned

A negative result, productively framed

The one-sentence summary
Today's large LLMs do not yet date Akkadian to philological standards — and our protocol shows why, with controls, rather than just reporting a low score.
They date on surface distribution, not learned structure
Random-weight Qwen ties the trained ones, and scale is flat from 1.7B to 120B — whatever lets them order texts is recoverable from architecture, not from learned Akkadian.
The win is the objective
A 400M model trained to translate Akkadian beats them all. Not tokenizer (it's the worst), not architecture (the base is at the floor), not next-token finetuning (a no-op) — the seq2seq/translation objective is what instills the signal.
The method is the contribution
The maximal-balanced PLS protocol — with its controls (random floor, NTP-null, tokenizer audit, balanced resampling) — is a reusable benchmark for separating apparent from causal dating ability.
Wrapping into a thesis

What is done, and where this sits

Done — ready to write up
(1) Unified 5-database corpus + cleaning pipeline. (2) The maximal-balanced PLS benchmark protocol. (3) The model comparison (TF-IDF / MLM / Qwen 1.7–32B / gpt-oss-120B / Thalesian / random). (4) The Thalesian autopsy: finetune, not tokenizer or architecture.
In progress
Manifold / geodesic structure of the embeddings; error-overlap analysis across models.
The thesis argument it all supports
“We show large LLMs cannot genuinely represent Akkadian diachronic change, build a controlled protocol that proves why, and identify the translation objective as the factor that does work.”
For discussion today
Which of these becomes the central chapter, and what is the minimum still missing to converge on a complete M.Sc. thesis (and a possible publication).
